14360:
Self-control is the ability to manage your own thoughts, emotions, urges, and behavior — especially when a part of you wants to do something that your better judgment says you shouldn't.

It is the internal power you use to stop yourself from doing something tempting but harmful, or to push yourself to do something difficult but worthwhile.

Think of it this way: inside you, there is often a conflict between two forces —

  • What you want right now (eat the cake, skip the workout, lash out in anger, stay in bed)
  • What you know is better for you (eat healthy, exercise, stay calm, wake up on time)

Self-control is what lets the second force win over the first.
Two Sides of Self-Control

Self-control works in two directions, and both are equally important:

1. Holding back (Inhibition)
This is stopping yourself from doing something you feel an impulse to do. Examples:

  • Not shouting at someone even though you're furious
  • Not checking your phone every five minutes when you're trying to focus
  • Not spending money on something you can't afford
  • Not eating junk food when you're trying to be healthy

2. Pushing forward (Persistence)
This is making yourself do something even when you don't feel like it. Examples:

  • Studying when you'd rather watch TV
  • Going to the gym when you feel lazy
  • Finishing a task even when it's boring
  • Waking up early even when your body wants to sleep

Both require the same underlying skill — overriding what feels easy or comfortable in the moment.
Self-Control Is About the Gap Between Feeling and Action

A key insight: self-control does not mean you stop feeling urges or desires. You still feel them. What changes is what you do with them.

A person with strong self-control still feels anger — they just don't act on it destructively.
A person with strong self-control still feels the temptation to eat the cake — they just choose not to.

This gap between feeling an impulse and acting on it is exactly where self-control lives.
Self-Control vs. Willpower vs. Discipline

These three words are often used interchangeably, but here's how they relate:

  • Willpower is the raw mental energy or force you use in a specific moment to resist an urge. It is short-term and can get depleted (you have more willpower in the morning than late at night after a tiring day).
  • Discipline refers to a consistent, structured habit of doing the right thing regularly, often built over time. Disciplined people rely less on willpower because good behavior becomes a routine.
  • Self-control is the broader concept that includes both — it is the overall capacity to regulate yourself, both in single moments (willpower) and over time (discipline). Self-control is the umbrella term.
What Self-Control Looks Like in Real Life

Self-control appears in almost every area of human life:

  • Eating: Choosing a salad over a burger when you're trying to be healthy
  • Spending: Not buying something on impulse even though you really want it
  • Anger: Staying calm in an argument instead of saying something hurtful
  • Work: Sitting down to finish a task instead of procrastinating
  • Relationships: Not saying something mean to a loved one just because you're in a bad mood
  • Addiction: Resisting cigarettes, alcohol, gambling, or social media when you're trying to quit
  • Sleep: Going to bed on time instead of scrolling your phone till 2 AM
Why Self-Control Is Hard

Self-control is genuinely difficult because of how the human mind is built. Your brain has two systems constantly in tension:

  • A fast, emotional, impulsive system — it wants pleasure now, it hates discomfort, and it reacts quickly. This system is very powerful.
  • A slow, rational, deliberate system — it thinks about long-term consequences and makes careful decisions. This system takes effort.

Self-control is essentially the rational system overriding the impulsive system. Because the impulsive system is fast and automatic, it often gets a head start. That's why temptation can feel almost automatic, while resisting it takes a conscious, effortful decision.
Self-Control Gets Weaker When You're Tired or Stressed

One of the most important things to know: self-control is like a muscle — it can get fatigued.

When you're exhausted, emotionally overwhelmed, hungry, or under a lot of stress, your ability to exercise self-control goes down. This is called ego depletion (using up your mental resources). That's why people eat poorly late at night, snap at others when they're stressed, or make bad decisions when they're tired.

This doesn't mean you're weak — it means self-control is a limited resource that needs to be managed wisely, not burned through carelessly.
Self-Control Is Also Like a Muscle — It Can Be Trained

The good news: just like a muscle, self-control can be strengthened with practice.

When you regularly practice small acts of self-control — keeping your room tidy, exercising a few times a week, resisting small temptations — your overall capacity for self-control grows over time. It becomes less effortful. Eventually, some of it becomes habit, so you don't even need to actively fight yourself anymore.
What Strong Self-Control Is Not

It's worth clearing up some common misunderstandings:

  • It is not suppressing all emotion. People with strong self-control still feel deeply — they just don't let their emotions drive every action.
  • It is not being cold or robotic. Self-control includes knowing when to let go and enjoy yourself.
  • It is not the same as perfectionism. You can have self-control and still fail sometimes — the key is getting back on track.
  • It is not about having no desires. Everyone has desires. Self-control is about which ones you choose to act on.
Why Self-Control Matters

Decades of research consistently show that people with higher self-control tend to do better in almost every area of life:

  • Better physical health (diet, exercise, avoiding harmful habits)
  • Better mental health (less anxiety, better emotional balance)
  • Better relationships (less conflict, more trust)
  • Better financial outcomes (saving money, avoiding debt)
  • Better academic and professional success (sustained effort pays off)

In short, self-control is one of the most powerful factors in living a good, intentional life — because it determines whether you are in charge of your actions, or whether your impulses are.
One-Line Summary
Self-control is the ability to pause between what you feel like doing and what you actually do — and choose wisely.
14361:
A self-effacing person is someone who deliberately makes themselves seem smaller, less important, or less noticeable than they actually are. They downplay their own abilities, achievements, and presence — not because they lack confidence in every area of life, but because they consciously choose not to draw attention to themselves.

Think of it this way: if you just gave a brilliant speech that received a standing ovation, a self-effacing response would be to say, "Oh, I just said a few words — anyone could have done it." You know it went well. You're choosing to erase that from the spotlight.
What it looks like in real life

Self-effacing behavior shows up in recognizable patterns:

  • Deflecting compliments ("It was really nothing special")
  • Giving credit to others even when you deserve it
  • Staying in the background even when you've earned a place at the front
  • Speaking about your achievements in the smallest possible terms
  • Not asserting your own needs, opinions, or value — even when it would be completely fair to do so

The key thing to notice is that this is active behavior. A self-effacing person is not merely quiet or reserved — they are actively working to reduce their own visibility.

The motivation matters, because it shapes whether the word carries a positive or negative shade:

  1. Genuine humility — Some people truly don't feel the need to be celebrated. They find satisfaction in the work itself, not the recognition.
  2. Cultural upbringing — In many cultures (especially in South and East Asia, for example), modesty is considered a virtue. Boasting is seen as rude, so people are raised to minimize themselves as a form of good manners.
  3. Social grace — A self-effacing person often wants to make others feel comfortable. By not dominating the room, they give space for everyone else.
  4. Insecurity — Sometimes self-effacing behavior comes from a belief that one doesn't truly deserve praise. This is a less healthy form of it.
  5. Politeness or professionalism — In formal settings, speaking modestly about yourself can be a sign of class and tact.
The positive and negative sides of the word

"Self-effacing" is generally a positive or neutral adjective. When you call someone self-effacing, you are usually paying them a subtle compliment — it suggests humility and an absence of arrogance, which most people find refreshing and likable.

However, taken too far, self-effacing behavior can become a problem. A person who never stands up for themselves, never claims credit, and always disappears into the background may be holding themselves back unfairly. In this case, the word can carry a note of quiet concern — as in, "She's talented, but she's too self-effacing to ever push for the promotion she deserves."

So the word sits in a range: mild self-effacement reads as charming modesty; extreme self-effacement reads as self-erasure.
How it differs from similar words

These words are neighbors, but they're not the same:

  • Humble — Humility is an internal quality: you don't believe you're better than others. Being self-effacing is behavioral: you actively show that in how you present yourself. A humble person might still accept praise graciously. A self-effacing person will almost always deflect it.
  • Modest — Modesty is very close to self-effacing, but slightly milder. Modest means you don't brag or exaggerate. Self-effacing goes a step further — you actively minimize yourself, often beyond what is strictly necessary.
  • Shy or introverted — Shyness is about social anxiety or discomfort. A self-effacing person may be entirely at ease socially — they choose to step back. The difference is choice versus inability.
  • Self-deprecating — This means making jokes or remarks at your own expense (e.g., laughing at your own mistakes in public). It's a specific type of self-effacing behavior, but self-effacing is broader. You can be self-effacing without being funny about it.

1. Despite having led the entire project from scratch, Ravi was self-effacing in the meeting, saying it had been "a team effort all the way."
  2. Her self-effacing manner made it easy to overlook just how accomplished she really was — she never once mentioned her PhD unless directly asked.
  3. He gave a self-effacing little laugh when his editor called the novel "brilliant" and said, "It's just something I scribbled on weekends."
  4. There's a fine line between being self-effacing and failing to advocate for yourself — at some point, you have to let people see your worth.

Self-effacing describes a person — or a moment, a remark, a smile — in which someone actively shrinks their own presence. It is the opposite of boastful, showy, or self-promoting. The word suggests a person who would rather the light fall on others than on themselves. Used in moderation, it is widely admired. Taken to an extreme, it can quietly work against a person.

If you meet someone who keeps saying "it was nothing" when it clearly was something, who credits everyone else when they did the work, and who steps out of photographs rather than into them — that person is self-effacing.
14362:
Self-governance is the ability of a person, group, or community to manage and direct their own affairs — making their own rules, decisions, and choices — without being controlled by an outside authority.

The word is built from two simple ideas: self (oneself, on one's own) and governance (the act of governing or controlling). Put together, it means: controlling yourself, or your group, from within — not from the outside.

Self-governance works at three distinct levels, and understanding each one makes the whole idea click.

1. Personal Self-Governance (The Individual)

At the personal level, self-governance means the ability to control your own behaviour, impulses, and decisions. It is the capacity to set your own standards and live by them — without needing someone else to force or supervise you.

A person who practises self-governance doesn't steal, not because a police officer is watching, but because they have internalized the rule that stealing is wrong. They show up to work on time, not because a boss is standing over them, but because they have decided that punctuality is important to them. They resist eating junk food at midnight, not because someone hid it from them, but because they regulate their own behaviour.

In this sense, self-governance is closely tied to discipline, responsibility, and moral maturity. A self-governing person is one who has moved beyond needing external enforcement and has developed the internal capacity to guide themselves.

2. Political Self-Governance (Nations and Peoples)

At the political level — and this is the most common and historically significant use of the word — self-governance refers to the right of a community, nation, or people to govern themselves, rather than being governed by a foreign power or an outside ruler.

When a colony breaks free from an empire and begins running its own affairs, it achieves self-governance. When a democratic country allows its citizens to elect their own representatives and make their own laws, that is self-governance. The opposite would be a situation where an outside force — a colonial empire, a foreign occupier, or a dictator who was never chosen by the people — makes all the decisions for a community.

Political self-governance rests on a few key ideas:

  • The people being governed have a say in how they are governed.
  • The rules come from within the community, not imposed from outside.
  • There is accountability — those who make decisions can be questioned, challenged, or removed.

India's independence movement, for example, was fundamentally a struggle for self-governance — the right of Indians to determine their own laws, leaders, and future, rather than having those decided in London.

3. Organisational or Community Self-Governance (Groups and Institutions)

Groups — a school, a professional body, a cooperative, a neighbourhood association — can also be self-governing. This means the group makes its own rules, enforces its own standards, and resolves its own problems without constant interference from a higher authority.

A self-governing school, for instance, might set its own curriculum and code of conduct, rather than having every rule dictated by the government. A self-governing professional association (like a bar council for lawyers or a medical council for doctors) sets its own ethical standards and disciplines members who violate them, rather than waiting for the government to step in every time.

Self-governance — at any level — doesn't just happen. It requires certain conditions to work:

Capacity: The person or group must actually be capable of making sound decisions. A self-governing nation needs educated, informed citizens. A self-governing individual needs the knowledge and maturity to make responsible choices.

Accountability: Self-governance is not the same as doing whatever you want with no consequences. A self-governing body is still answerable — to its own members, to its own rules, or to its own conscience. The difference is that the accountability comes from within the system, not from an external master.

Legitimacy: The rules and decisions made must be accepted as valid by those they apply to. In a self-governing democracy, laws are legitimate because the people themselves (through elections and representatives) had a hand in creating them.

Willingness to take responsibility: Self-governance means accepting that if things go wrong, you cannot simply blame an outside ruler. The responsibility belongs to you or your group.

It helps to see how self-governance sits alongside a few words it is often confused with.

Autonomy is very close in meaning — it is the freedom to act independently. But autonomy is more about the freedom you have, while self-governance is more about what you do with that freedom — the actual act of running your own affairs responsibly.

Self-rule is essentially a synonym, used especially in the political sense. Self-governance is slightly broader because it applies to personal and organisational life too.

Self-control is the personal dimension of self-governance — specifically about managing your own impulses and behaviour. Self-governance is the bigger concept; self-control is one part of it.

Independence refers to the condition of not being controlled by others. Self-governance is what you do after you are independent — the active management of your own affairs.

Anarchy is sometimes confused with self-governance, but they are very different. Anarchy means the absence of any governing authority. Self-governance means governing yourself — it still involves rules, order, and responsibility; the difference is that these come from within rather than being imposed from outside.
A Few Clear Examples to Cement It

• A nation holding free elections and choosing its own government is exercising political self-governance.
  • A student who studies regularly without parents nagging them is demonstrating personal self-governance.
  • A village council that manages its own water supply, settles local disputes, and collects its own contributions — without waiting for city authorities to do everything — is practising community self-governance.
  • A professional guild that creates its own code of ethics and expels members who violate it is an example of organisational self-governance.

Self-governance is considered one of the highest ideals in both political philosophy and personal development — for the same underlying reason: it reflects the belief that human beings are capable of directing themselves wisely, and that this capacity deserves to be respected and protected.

In politics, the argument for self-governance is that people understand their own conditions, needs, and values better than a distant ruler ever can. Imposing governance from the outside is not just inefficient — it is a violation of dignity.

In personal life, the ideal of self-governance reflects the view that a truly mature, free human being is one who has internalized good values and acts on them independently — not because of fear, but because of genuine understanding and choice.

This is why self-governance is not just a political term. It is a word that sits at the heart of what it means to be free, responsible, and mature — whether you are an individual, a community, or a nation.
14363:
A self-important person believes they are more significant, more authoritative, or more worthy of attention than they actually are — and they show this belief through the way they speak and behave. The key word is "important." It is specifically about an exaggerated, inflated sense of one's own significance or weight in the world.

This is not just quiet, private pride. The person acts out this belief. They carry themselves as if their presence matters enormously, as if their words deserve unusual respect, and as if their time is especially precious.

Self-important is a negative, critical word. When you call someone self-important, you are saying:

"This person thinks they are a very big deal — but they are not as important as they believe."

There is a quiet mockery in the word. You are not impressed by them. You see through their inflated self-presentation. It is a word used to gently ridicule someone's exaggerated sense of self.
What a Self-Important Person Actually Does

This is where the word really comes to life. A self-important person may:

  • Speak in a slow, deliberate, formal tone as if every word they say deserves to be written down
  • Expect others to take them seriously even in minor, casual situations
  • Act easily offended when they are not given the respect they feel they deserve
  • Dismiss or talk over others, as if their own opinions carry far more weight
  • Use grand or pompous language even when plain words would do perfectly fine
  • Treat routine tasks — like sending an email or attending a small meeting — as if they are very weighty matters
  • Expect special treatment — a better seat, the first word in a conversation, or others rearranging their plans around them
A Picture to Lock It In

Imagine a person who works in a small local office. One day, they are asked to review a minor document. They walk into the room dramatically, set their folder down with great ceremony, clear their throat, and begin speaking very slowly: "I have reviewed this document carefully, and I have some important thoughts I'd like to share."

The document is two paragraphs long. Their "important thoughts" are ordinary suggestions any colleague could have made. But they behave as if they are a senior advisor delivering a verdict of great consequence.

That is self-important behavior.
How It Differs from Similar Words

These words are related, but each has a slightly different flavour:

Arrogant — An arrogant person feels superior to others and may be dismissive or even rude about it. Arrogance is about feeling above others. Self-importance is more specifically about feeling like you are a big deal — a person of weight and significance.

Pompous — Very close to self-important, but "pompous" focuses more on the outward style — the grand, showy, overly formal way someone speaks or presents themselves. A self-important person is often pompous, but self-importance is the belief, while pompousness is more the manner.

Conceited — Conceit is usually about being excessively proud of one's personal qualities, looks, or talents. Self-importance is more specifically about one's role, status, or authority.

Vain — Vanity is about excessive pride in one's appearance or achievements, often tied to wanting flattery and admiration. Self-importance is less about wanting to be admired for beauty and more about demanding to be taken seriously.

Egotistical — An egotistical person is excessively focused on themselves — talking about themselves constantly. Self-importance has a more institutional quality: it is about how much one believes their position or role matters, not just their personal qualities.

• The new manager was so self-important that he sent a calendar invitation for what turned out to be a two-minute phone call.
  • She gave a self-important little speech before the team was allowed to start eating at the company lunch.
  • He spoke in a self-important tone, as if the question of which route to take on the road trip required his expert judgment.
  • The local councillor was deeply self-important — he expected shopkeepers to recognise him by name and treat him accordingly.
  • I found his email exhausting to read; every sentence was written in that self-important style where even a simple update sounds like a declaration.

Self-importance (noun) — the quality or attitude of being self-important.
Her self-importance was obvious the moment she walked in and expected everyone to stop what they were doing.

Self-importantly (adverb) — in a self-important manner.
He self-importantly announced that he had a "prior engagement," when in fact he was going home to watch television.
When and Where You'd Use This Word

You can use "self-important" in everyday conversation, in writing, in criticism, or in informal and semi-formal contexts. It is not slang, nor is it overly formal. It suits an email, an essay, a novel, or a casual remark equally well.

You would typically use it to:

  • Describe someone's personality or manner
  • Criticise the behaviour of a person in a position of minor authority who acts as if their authority is vast
  • Gently mock someone's exaggerated seriousness about themselves
A self-important person is someone who has quietly decided they matter more than the world has confirmed — and behaves accordingly.
14364:
Self-indulgence means the act of freely giving yourself whatever you want — pleasure, comfort, or satisfaction — especially without holding back, without worrying about whether it's good for you, and often without caring much about consequences.

The key word inside it is indulge, which means to allow yourself (or someone else) to have or do something enjoyable, especially something you normally restrict. When you add self- to it, you are both the one doing the allowing and the one being allowed. You are treating yourself.
What makes something "self-indulgence" and not just "enjoyment"?

Simple enjoyment is neutral — you enjoy a sunny afternoon, a good conversation, a glass of water when you're thirsty. That's just living.

Self-indulgence carries a shade of meaning beyond plain enjoyment. It suggests:

  • Excess or lack of restraint — going a little (or a lot) further than you "should"
  • Prioritizing your own pleasure over discipline, responsibility, or the needs of others
  • A choice — you're consciously letting yourself go, rather than simply feeling happy

For example, eating one piece of chocolate is enjoyment. Eating the entire box, knowing you shouldn't, while ignoring your diet — that is self-indulgence.

Self-indulgence exists on a wide spectrum.

Mild, harmless self-indulgence — things most people relate to and smile at:

  • Spending an entire Sunday watching your favourite TV show instead of doing chores
  • Buying an expensive dessert you didn't need
  • Taking a long, luxurious bath for no particular reason
  • Sleeping in on a holiday when you could have been productive

Moderate self-indulgence — where consequences start to show:

  • Regularly spending money on luxuries you can't quite afford
  • Eating unhealthily because it feels good in the moment
  • Procrastinating on important work to do things you enjoy more

Serious self-indulgence — where it becomes a real flaw or problem:

  • A leader so focused on personal comfort and power that they neglect their duties
  • Someone so absorbed in their own pleasures that they ignore people depending on them
  • An artist who keeps writing long, rambling passages in their book because they enjoy it, without thinking about whether the reader needs all of it

This is one of the most interesting things about this word — it depends on context and degree.

When people use it disapprovingly (the more common use):
They mean someone is being weak-willed, selfish, or irresponsible. They're saying: "You're prioritising your own comfort or pleasure when you shouldn't be." It suggests a lack of self-control or maturity.

"His self-indulgence was his downfall — he never learned to delay gratification."

"The film suffers from the director's self-indulgence; every scene goes on far too long."

When people use it approvingly or gently (less common, but real):
Sometimes it's used warmly, suggesting a harmless, well-deserved treat. Here, the tone is affectionate or even encouraging.

"Go on, it's your birthday — a little self-indulgence is perfectly fine."

"I know it's self-indulgence, but I bought myself fresh flowers for no reason."

The difference between these two uses is almost entirely about degree and circumstance. Small pleasures taken occasionally = acceptable, even charming. Excessive, repeated, or selfish pursuit of pleasure at others' expense = a character flaw.
Self-indulgence in creative and intellectual contexts

This word is used heavily when talking about art, writing, music, and film. Here, self-indulgence means a creator who follows their own preferences too freely — including things that they love but that make the work worse or harder for the audience.

A self-indulgent novel might have pages and pages of a character's inner thoughts that the author found fascinating but that slow the story to a crawl.

A self-indulgent musician might play a 20-minute guitar solo that serves their own ego more than the song.

The criticism here is: you forgot about your audience and just pleased yourself.

To sharpen the word further, it helps to know what it doesn't mean:

  • It is not simply enjoying yourself. Joy and self-indulgence are different — joy can be pure and clean; self-indulgence has a flavour of excess or surrender to it.
  • It is not self-care, which involves taking care of your wellbeing in a responsible, intentional way. Self-care is healthy. Self-indulgence tends toward the opposite.
  • It is not greed, though the two can overlap. Greed is specifically about wanting more (especially material things). Self-indulgence is broader — it's about giving yourself whatever feels good, in any domain.
  • It is not selfishness, though again they can overlap. Selfishness means disregarding others for your own benefit. Self-indulgence is more about surrendering to your own desires — others may or may not be affected.

One subtle quality of self-indulgence is that the person often knows they're doing it. There's a small awareness — sometimes guilty, sometimes cheerful — that you are letting yourself go.

When someone says "I know, I know — this is complete self-indulgence," they are acknowledging that they are choosing pleasure over better judgment. That self-awareness is baked into the word.

• "The autobiography was full of self-indulgence — she spent 80 pages writing about her childhood cat."
  • "After months of hard work, she felt that one week of self-indulgence was well-earned."
  • "His self-indulgence at the buffet left him feeling sick for the rest of the evening."
  • "The politician's self-indulgence — the private jet, the expensive suits paid for by public money — eventually cost him his career."
  • "There's a healthy kind of self-indulgence: treating yourself to something small that brings you genuine happiness without hurting anyone."

Self-indulgence is the act of freely allowing yourself to have or do what pleases you — especially beyond what is wise, restrained, or responsible — with the understanding that you are choosing your own pleasure or satisfaction, sometimes at the cost of discipline, others, or quality.
14365:
Self-mutilating describes something — most often a person, animal, or behavior — that involves deliberately causing serious physical damage, injury, or disfigurement to one's own body.

To understand it fully, take the two parts separately:

  • Mutilating means causing severe physical damage — cutting, tearing, burning, removing, or disfiguring a body part to the point where it is seriously injured or permanently altered.
  • Self- means that the one doing the damage and the one receiving it are the same. There is no outside force. The harm is inflicted inward, on oneself.

Put together: self-mutilating = causing severe physical harm to one's own body, deliberately.
What Makes It Different From Simply "Hurting Yourself"

This is an important distinction. Everyday self-harm (like accidentally cutting your finger, or biting your nails too hard) is not what this word captures. Self-mutilating carries a much heavier weight. It implies:

  1. Intentionality — the action is done on purpose, not by accident.
  2. Severity — the damage is significant: it disfigures, wounds deeply, or destroys. "Mutilate" is a strong word. A small scratch is not mutilation. Serious cutting, burning, gouging, or removing a part of the body — that is.
  3. Directed inward — the harm is aimed at oneself, making it both the cause and the victim simultaneously.
Where and How the Word Is Used

1. In psychology and medicine (most common usage)

This is where you will most frequently encounter the word. "Self-mutilating behavior" or "self-mutilating tendencies" refers to a pattern of deliberately injuring one's own body, often as a response to emotional pain, trauma, or severe psychological distress.

People who engage in self-mutilating behavior may cut their skin, burn themselves, or inflict other serious wounds. It is considered a symptom of certain mental health conditions, such as borderline personality disorder, severe depression, or trauma-related disorders.

"The therapist noted the patient's self-mutilating behavior had worsened during periods of extreme stress."

"The clinic developed a program specifically for adolescents with self-mutilating tendencies."

It is worth noting that in clinical settings, professionals sometimes use the term non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) alongside or instead of "self-mutilating," because the latter can sound stigmatizing — but "self-mutilating" remains widely used in formal writing and diagnosis.

2. In animal behavior and biology

Animals under extreme stress, pain, illness, or psychological deprivation (such as being kept in cruel or unnatural conditions) can also exhibit self-mutilating behavior — biting their own skin, pulling out their feathers (in birds), scratching wounds open, and so on.

"The zoo reported self-mutilating behavior in the caged parrot, a known sign of chronic psychological stress."

3. In a figurative or metaphorical sense

Less commonly, but still correctly, the word can describe an organization, system, group, or entity that is destroying itself through its own decisions or actions — as if cutting itself from within.

"The company's self-mutilating policies — slashing its best talent while expanding recklessly — led to its collapse within two years."

Here, no literal body is being harmed, but the spirit of the word is preserved: the damage is severe, deliberate (or at least self-caused), and directed inward.
The Nuance of Severity — Why "Mutilating" and Not Just "Harming"

The choice of the root word mutilate is deliberate and significant. Consider this spectrum:

  • Hurting yourself → vague, can be minor.
  • Harming yourself → suggests meaningful damage, but still broad.
  • Injuring yourself → implies a wound, but could be accidental.
  • Mutilating yourself → implies serious, disfiguring, severe damage, and almost always carries the sense of intentionality.

So when you call something "self-mutilating," you are signaling that the damage involved is not trivial. It is grave, often visible, and significantly alters the body or structure in question.
Grammatical Usage (How to Use It in a Sentence)

As an adjective, "self-mutilating" always describes a noun. It cannot stand alone as a complete thought. Here's how it typically pairs:

  • Self-mutilating behavior — the most common pairing; describes a pattern of actions.
  • Self-mutilating tendencies — a person's inclination toward such behavior.
  • Self-mutilating actions/acts — specific instances.
  • Self-mutilating individual/patient — a person who engages in such behavior (used clinically, though sometimes considered harsh in informal settings).

"Her self-mutilating behavior began in her early teens and continued into adulthood."

"The researcher studied self-mutilating animals to understand the psychological effects of isolation."

Since you want a complete understanding, here are the other grammatical forms of the same word family:

  • Self-mutilate (verb): "She would self-mutilate when overwhelmed." — the act itself.
  • Self-mutilation (noun): "Self-mutilation is recognized as a psychiatric symptom." — the condition or act as a thing.
  • Self-mutilator (noun): "He was identified as a self-mutilator by the clinical team." — the person who performs the act.

All of these share the same core idea: deliberate, severe self-inflicted physical damage.

Self-mutilating describes a person, animal, behavior, or (figuratively) a system that deliberately inflicts serious, disfiguring physical harm upon itself — combining the inward direction of "self" with the severity and destructiveness of "mutilate."
14366:
Self-pity is the feeling of being excessively sorry for yourself — dwelling on your own suffering, misfortune, or troubles in a way that goes beyond what the situation truly deserves.

To understand it, break the word in two. Pity is the sadness you feel for someone who is suffering. Self- means that feeling is pointed inward, at yourself. So self-pity is essentially: I feel deeply, deeply sorry for me.

When someone experiences self-pity, a few things are usually happening at once. They are focused almost entirely on how bad their own situation is. They feel like a victim — like life has treated them unfairly, or worse than it treats other people. And they tend to stay in that feeling instead of moving through it. Phrases like "Why does this always happen to me?" or "Nobody understands how much I suffer" are the inner voice of self-pity.

It also often carries a quiet wish: for others to notice the suffering and feel sympathy for it.
Why It Has a Negative Connotation

Self-pity is not a neutral word. It almost always carries a negative or critical tone. When you say someone is "feeling self-pity," you are implying that their sadness has become excessive, self-indulgent, or unproductive. You're suggesting they are wallowing — the way an animal rolls around in mud and can't seem to get out.

Importantly, the pain that triggered self-pity can be completely real. The problem isn't that the suffering is fake. The problem is the response to that suffering: it has become too inward, too prolonged, and too focused on victimhood rather than healing or action.

Think of it this way: normal sadness is a healthy emotional response to something painful. Self-pity is what happens when that sadness curdles — when it stops being a natural reaction and becomes a place someone lives in.
How It Differs from Normal Sadness or Grief

This is a crucial distinction. Not every sad feeling is self-pity, and calling someone's grief "self-pity" can itself be unfair.

Healthy grief sounds like: "This is really painful. I'm hurting and I need time."

Self-pity sounds like: "Everything always goes wrong for me. My life is harder than everyone else's. Nobody really cares. I deserve to suffer like this."

The key differences are: self-pity tends to exaggerate, it tends to last far longer than healthy grieving, it frames the person as uniquely cursed or victimized, and it is passive — there is no desire to heal, act, or move forward. Healthy sadness, by contrast, eventually moves toward acceptance or action.
Common Phrases You'll Hear With This Word

Knowing how a word is actually used in conversation is just as important as knowing its definition.

"Wallow in self-pity" is the most common phrase. To wallow means to roll around in something helplessly. So "wallowing in self-pity" means someone is deeply submerged in feeling sorry for themselves and making no effort to come out of it.

"A fit of self-pity" means a sudden, intense episode of the feeling — often short-lived but dramatic.

"Sink into self-pity" suggests a gradual slide into the feeling, as though being pulled downward.

"Full of self-pity" describes someone whose whole attitude or outlook is colored by this feeling.

"After failing the exam, she spent the whole week wallowing in self-pity instead of preparing for a resit."

"His memoir is refreshingly free of self-pity — he writes about his hardships with calm honesty."

"Stop the self-pity and let's figure out what to do next."

"It's easy to sink into self-pity when things fall apart, but it rarely makes things better."

"There was a note of self-pity in his voice when he talked about how no one supported him."

Self-pitying (adjective) — used to describe a person, attitude, tone, or behavior that shows self-pity. "He had a self-pitying look on his face." / "She wrote in a self-pitying way that made it hard to sympathize."

Self-pityingly (adverb) — used to describe how someone does or says something. "He sighed self-pityingly and stared out the window."
One Final Way to Remember It

If you ever want a quick mental image to anchor this word: picture someone sitting in the corner of a room, arms crossed, convinced that their life is harder than anyone else's, not wanting advice or solutions — just wanting the world to see how much they are suffering. That portrait is self-pity in action.

It is a very human feeling — nearly everyone experiences it sometimes. But as a word, it is almost always used as a criticism, pointing out when someone has let that feeling take over in a way that is excessive and unproductive.
14367:
When you possess something, you own it and have control over it. Self-possessed takes that idea and applies it to a person's own inner world — their emotions, reactions, and behavior. A self-possessed person, in a sense, owns themselves. Their feelings don't run away from them. They don't get flustered, rattled, or swept away by pressure, stress, or strong emotions. They stay in command of themselves.

In plain terms: a self-possessed person is calm, controlled, and confident in a quiet, natural way — especially when it matters most.

The key to understanding this word is the phrase "especially under pressure." Almost anyone can appear calm when life is easy. What makes someone self-possessed is how they behave when things get hard — when they're being criticized, questioned, surprised, embarrassed, or put on the spot.

A self-possessed person in those moments:

  • Doesn't panic or visibly lose control
  • Doesn't become defensive, flustered, or desperate
  • Speaks clearly and steadily
  • Carries themselves with poise and quiet confidence
  • Responds to situations rather than reacting to them

It's like watching someone walk through a storm without looking rattled.

Self-possessed suggests something settled and stable from the inside. It's not a performance. It's not someone gritting their teeth and forcing themselves to look calm. It's a person who seems genuinely at ease within themselves — grounded, centered, and secure.

This is why it's often used to describe people who come across as mature beyond their years — a young person who handles a difficult situation with an astonishing degree of composure. The word carries quiet admiration.

This word is often confused with nearby ideas, so let's draw clear lines:

  • Not emotionless. A self-possessed person feels things fully — fear, excitement, grief, joy — but doesn't get controlled by those feelings. The feelings don't spill over and take the wheel.
  • Not arrogant or cold. It's not about superiority or aloofness. A self-possessed person can be warm and open — they simply don't fall apart under pressure.
  • Not forced calm. If someone is visibly suppressing panic and barely holding together, that is not self-possession. The quality has an effortless quality to it, like it comes naturally.
  • Not the same as silence. A self-possessed person can speak boldly, laugh, engage — they just do it without losing their internal footing.
How It Differs from Similar Words

These words are close cousins, but each has its own shade:

  • Composed — calm at a particular moment. It's more situational. You can become composed after a shock. Self-possessed is more of a deep-rooted trait.
  • Poised — graceful and balanced, especially in social situations. Poise is a bit more about outward elegance. Self-possession goes deeper, into psychological control.
  • Collected — keeping yourself together, usually in a specific stressful moment. "She was collected during the interview." Similar, but again more situational than self-possessed.
  • Confident — belief in your own abilities. Confidence is about what you can do. Self-possession is about how well you handle yourself.
  • Self-controlled — actively restraining impulses. This has a strained, deliberate flavor to it. Self-possession feels more natural and effortless.

Of all of these, poised and composed come closest — but self-possessed is the richest and most complete of the group.

1. "The young lawyer walked into the crowded courtroom looking completely self-possessed, as if the pressure of the trial didn't touch her at all."
  2. "Despite being caught off guard by the reporter's sharp question, he remained self-possessed and gave a measured, thoughtful answer."
  3. "There was something self-possessed about her — even at eighteen, she never seemed thrown by difficult people or difficult situations."
  4. "He handled the job interview in a self-possessed way that made him seem far more experienced than he was."

Notice how in each case, the person is in a situation that could cause anxiety, panic, or defensiveness — but they aren't rattled by it. That is the word's heartland.

Self-possessed is a formal, literary word. You'll encounter it more in written English — novels, journalism, biographies, essays — than in casual spoken conversation. When someone uses it, they're paying a person a subtle compliment: this person has a quiet, admirable mastery over themselves.

It most commonly describes adults, but its impact is sharpest when used for someone young, or someone in a situation where you would expect them to be unsettled — because then the calmness becomes truly remarkable.
Self-possessed describes a person who is in full, natural control of their emotions and behavior — calm, confident, and unshakeable — particularly when circumstances are difficult or high-pressure.
14368:
When someone is self-righteous, they are deeply convinced that they are morally good, morally correct, and morally superior — and they make sure other people feel it.

The key word here is "self". The righteousness is self-appointed. They have crowned themselves the judge of what is right and wrong, and they look down on people who don't meet their standard.

It is not just a private feeling. A self-righteous person shows this sense of moral superiority — through their tone, their words, their attitude, and their behaviour. That outward display is what makes it so irritating to others.

Imagine a person who:

  • Believes their own values and moral choices are the correct ones
  • Judges others for not sharing those values
  • Acts as though they are on a higher moral level than everyone around them
  • Lectures, preaches, or speaks down to people about right and wrong
  • Feels a smug satisfaction in their own goodness

That person is self-righteous.

The word always carries a negative meaning. Nobody thinks of themselves as self-righteous — it is always a label others use to criticise someone. When you call a person self-righteous, you are saying: "You think you're better than everyone else, and it shows."
What Makes It Different From Just "Being Right"

This is a subtle but very important distinction.

A self-righteous person might actually be correct about the moral issue. That is not the problem. The problem is their attitude.

Consider two people who don't eat meat:

Person A quietly follows their diet. If someone asks why, they explain simply. They don't judge others who eat meat.

Person B constantly brings up how wrong it is to eat meat. They make faces when others order a burger. They share long posts about other people's moral failures. At dinner, they say, "I could never eat that. I actually care about animals."

Person B might be factually correct about the harm done to animals. But Person B is self-righteous. The issue is not what they believe — it is the condescension, the preachiness, and the pleasure they take in feeling morally above others.

This distinction matters a lot: self-righteousness is about attitude and behaviour, not about whether the person is actually right or wrong.

A self-righteous person:

1. Has a blind spot about themselves. They judge others harshly while failing to examine their own flaws. They hold others to a standard they don't apply to themselves — or if they do apply it to themselves, they are certain they pass the test perfectly. This selective vision is at the heart of self-righteousness.

2. Finds identity in being "good." Their sense of self-worth comes heavily from seeing themselves as morally superior. This is why they are so uncomfortable around people who make different choices — those people feel like a threat to their identity.

3. Lacks genuine empathy. Because they've already decided what is right, they are unwilling to truly understand why others might think, choose, or live differently. They replace curiosity with judgment.

4. Often performs their morality. The goodness is not just private — it needs to be seen. There's a certain show involved. They want credit for being the good one in the room.
What It Looks, Sounds, and Feels Like

Here are some real-life examples to make it vivid:

  • A very religious person who frequently reminds others that they are sinners and that they themselves are living righteously.
  • A fitness-obsessed person who makes comments like, "I'd never put that into my body," when others eat junk food.
  • A politically passionate person who treats anyone with a different view as not just wrong, but morally corrupt — and says so loudly and repeatedly.
  • A person who, whenever a moral issue comes up, cannot resist letting everyone know exactly where they stand and how their position is the only decent one.
  • Someone who, after others have apologised or reflected on a mistake, continues to remind them of it repeatedly — savouring the moment of moral advantage.

The feeling you get around a self-righteous person is usually one of being judged, lectured, or made to feel guilty. There is a heaviness to their presence on moral topics. Conversations with them have a kind of sermon quality. You feel that they are waiting for you to fall short so they can confirm their own superiority.

The tone of "self-righteous" is critical and somewhat contemptuous. It is a word used to put someone in their place — to say that their moral confidence has crossed into arrogance.

Closely related expressions that carry a similar meaning:

  • Sanctimonious — very similar to self-righteous; often implies that the person is also somewhat hypocritical (preaching values they don't fully live by themselves)
  • Holier-than-thou — an informal phrase meaning exactly the same thing; "You act as if you are holier than everyone else"
  • Preachy — focused specifically on the behaviour of lecturing or moralising repeatedly
  • Smug — pleased with oneself in a way others find irritating; broader than moral matters but overlaps here
An Important Nuance: The Hypocrisy Connection

Self-righteous people are often hypocrites, but not always. Sometimes they genuinely do live by the values they preach. The hypocrisy, when it exists, makes the self-righteousness far worse in the eyes of others — there is nothing more grating than someone who moralises while failing to meet their own standards.

But even when there is no hypocrisy — when the person truly practices what they preach — the self-righteousness still exists in the way they treat others: the condescension, the judgment, the refusal to grant others the right to live differently.

To sharpen the definition, it helps to know what it does not mean:

  • Having strong moral beliefs — not self-righteous by itself. Many deeply ethical people are humble and non-judgmental.
  • Calling out genuinely harmful behaviour — pointing out actual wrongdoing clearly and firmly is not self-righteousness. It becomes self-righteous when it tips into superiority and contempt.
  • Being consistent — living by your values quietly is not self-righteous. It is the broadcasting and the judging that makes it so.

Here are some example sentences to see how the word is used naturally:

  • "He had a self-righteous tone whenever the topic of money came up, as if people who struggled financially simply lacked discipline."
  • "Her speech would have been more effective if it hadn't sounded so self-righteous — she kept implying that anyone who disagreed was a bad person."
  • "I agree with his values, but his self-righteous attitude makes it impossible to have a real conversation with him."
  • "There's a difference between being principled and being self-righteous. One earns respect; the other breeds resentment."

If you had to capture the whole word in one sentence:

A self-righteous person is someone who is so convinced of their own moral goodness that they look down on others and make sure those others feel their judgment — without recognising the arrogance in doing so.

That is the word, fully and accurately.
14369:
Self-sufficient means: able to provide for your own needs without depending on others.

Think of it in two parts:

  • "Self" = on your own, from within yourself
  • "Sufficient" = enough

Put them together: you have enough from within yourself. You don't need to go outside — to other people, places, or systems — to get what you need. Everything necessary is already there, or you can produce it yourself.
A Simple Picture

Imagine two farmers:

Farmer A buys all his vegetables from the market, pays someone to fix his tools, and relies on the city's water supply. He depends on many outside sources just to get through the day.

Farmer B grows her own vegetables, fixes her own tools, and collects rainwater from her roof. She meets her own needs without depending on others.

Farmer B is self-sufficient. She can keep going even if the market closes or no one comes to help her.
What "Needs" Can Mean

The word is flexible. The needs it refers to depend on the context:

  • Physical needs: food, water, shelter, energy
  • Financial needs: money, income
  • Emotional needs: reassurance, validation, support
  • Operational needs (for a system or organization): resources, inputs, power

The word applies whenever a person, group, place, or system can meet its own specific kind of need from within itself.
How It's Used in Different Contexts

1. A Person

A person is self-sufficient when they can manage their life — practically, financially, or emotionally — without leaning on others.

"After moving to a new city alone, she learned to be completely self-sufficient."

This means she handled her finances, daily tasks, and decisions on her own, without needing others to prop her up.

2. A Country or Region

A country is self-sufficient (in a particular area) when it can produce enough of something — food, energy, goods — without needing to import it.

"Norway is largely self-sufficient in energy because of its oil reserves and hydropower."

This means Norway doesn't need to buy energy from other countries.

3. A Community or Household

"The eco-village aimed to be self-sufficient by growing its own food and generating solar power."

The community wanted to meet all its basic needs from within itself, with no reliance on the outside world.

4. Emotionally (a person's inner life)

"He was emotionally self-sufficient — he didn't need constant approval from others to feel confident."

This means his sense of wellbeing came from within, not from external validation.

5. A System or Technology

"The satellite was designed to be self-sufficient, drawing all its power from solar panels."

The satellite doesn't need anything from outside to keep running.
It's a Spectrum, Not a Switch

Self-sufficiency isn't all-or-nothing. Very few people or things are perfectly self-sufficient in every way. The word is usually used to mean mostly or substantially able to meet one's own needs.

You might also hear it in a specific area:

"The country is self-sufficient in wheat but imports most of its oil."

Here, it doesn't mean total independence — just independence in that one area.
What Self-Sufficient Does NOT Mean

This is important, because learners often misunderstand it:

It does NOT mean:

  • Antisocial or unfriendly. A self-sufficient person can still enjoy friends, family, and relationships. It just means they don't need those relationships to survive or function.
  • Refusing all help. It means you can manage without help — not that you always reject it. A self-sufficient person who breaks their leg will still go to a doctor.
  • Wealthy. A person can be self-sufficient and have very little money, as long as they can meet their own needs in other ways (growing food, bartering, etc.).
  • Isolated or cut off. Self-sufficiency is about capability, not about being physically separated from the world.
The Feeling the Word Carries

Self-sufficient is almost always a positive word. It carries strong connotations of:

  • Capability — you're skilled and resourceful
  • Resilience — you can keep going even when outside support disappears
  • Freedom — you're not at the mercy of others
  • Maturity — you don't burden others unnecessarily

However, in rare cases, it can carry a slightly negative tone — if someone is so self-sufficient that they refuse help they genuinely need, or become emotionally unavailable to those who care about them. But this is the exception, not the rule.
Close Cousins: Words That Look Similar

Understanding these related words will sharpen your understanding of self-sufficient:

Self-reliant — Very close in meaning. The small difference: self-sufficient focuses on having enough within yourself (a state). Self-reliant focuses on the habit of relying on yourself rather than others (a behavior). In practice, the two are often used interchangeably.

Independent — Broader. It means free from control or influence of others in a general sense. A country can be politically independent (not ruled by another country) but still not self-sufficient (needing to import all its food and oil). So independence and self-sufficiency are related but not the same.

Self-sustaining — Similar, but used more for systems, processes, and organizations than for people. A self-sustaining fire feeds itself. A self-sustaining business generates enough revenue to cover all its costs without outside funding.

Autonomous — Means self-governing: making your own rules and decisions. It overlaps with self-sufficient in some uses but is more about decision-making than need-meeting.
Antonyms (Opposites)

OppositeWhat it means
DependentRelies on others to function or survive
ReliantNeeds outside support
NeedyRequires constant help or reassurance (often emotional)
Examples in Sentences

"After losing her job, she was grateful she had always been self-sufficient — she had savings, a vegetable garden, and the skills to manage on her own."

"The goal of the program is to make rural communities self-sufficient so they don't depend on government aid."

"She was intellectually self-sufficient — she rarely needed anyone to tell her what to think."

"The spacecraft was entirely self-sufficient, requiring no resupply missions from Earth."

"Growing up in a large, busy family taught him to be self-sufficient from a young age."
The One-Line Summary
Self-sufficient = able to meet your own needs from within yourself, without depending on outside people, sources, or support.
